notes:
Middleware Fix

  1. Fixed the middleware to allow unauthenticated access to the OpenAPI spec route for the mockup upload tool — without this, Open WebUI could not load the tool definition during admin setup, blocking tool registration entirely.

End-to-End Upload Testing

  1. Tested the new headless upload tool end-to-end by uploading a mockup file directly to the StackShift demo repository through the API, confirming the integration between Open WebUI and the CiteForge upload endpoint was working correctly.
  2. Reverted the test upload afterward to keep the repository clean — the file was only needed to verify the upload feature worked, not to stay as a permanent mockup.

name: Headless Upload Verification and Middleware Correction

notes:
API Feature Development

  1. Built a headless upload mode into the existing mockup upload endpoint so the Open WebUI chat operator can upload HTML files directly from a conversation using a GitHub access token — no login or CiteForge session required.
  2. Added file size validation and collision detection to the upload endpoint — files over 5 MB are rejected with a clear error, files between 1 and 5 MB upload but warn the operator they are too large for the migration to read, and name collisions return a flag rather than silently overwriting the existing file.

OpenAPI Integration

  1. Created an OpenAPI JSON specification for the upload endpoint so it can be registered in Open WebUI's admin panel as an external tool connection.
  2. Restructured the OpenAPI spec from a plain static file into a proper Next.js API route so it is always served from a predictable URL as part of the running application.
  3. Updated the authentication middleware to allow unauthenticated access to the OpenAPI spec route — required for Open WebUI to load the tool definition without needing a login session.

Operator Documentation

  1. Wrote a full admin setup guide covering how to register the upload tool in Open WebUI, what GitHub token scope is required, and how to attach the tool to the migration operator model.
  2. Updated the migration operator's skill document and prompts reference to describe the new upload tool, its parameters, collision behavior, and file size limits so the assistant can use and explain it correctly.
  3. Wrote the task specification recording the two-mode design decision (CiteForge UI mode vs. headless API mode), the testing checklist, rollback plan, and a complete implementation summary.

notes: The day centered on getting the chat-based migration assistant reliable access to the project repository. A persistent access failure was traced to a credential difference between two assistant presets rather than their tooling, and was resolved through the chat platform's admin settings — after which the assistant read the repository correctly and listed all fifteen mockup files. In parallel, the repository's move to a new GitHub organization was verified and absorbed: the local working copy, the documentation, the assistant instructions, and a lookup bug that could have resolved the repository to the wrong owner were all corrected. The migration workflow itself was upgraded and live-tested so runs can use the tested prompt stored in the repository, with the callback secret configured and the test run cancelled early on purpose to save cost. The day closed with the dispatch design settled and a step-by-step setup guide written for enabling chat-driven migrations.

notes:
1. Worked out how repository access should work across the company's two organizations, since a single access token cannot cover both.
  2. Chose one shared read-only token per organization rather than one per project, on the grounds that the extra isolation was not worth the ongoing management overhead.
  3. Identified a simpler alternative worth trying first, which removes access tokens entirely by having each person sign in with their own account.
  4. Established that installing a company-wide application on both organizations does not solve the problem in this setup, because those credentials expire hourly and cannot be refreshed automatically.
  5. Discovered the existing migration service already lists page mockups across both organizations, which means the planned service connection removes the access problem altogether at the next stage.
  6. Set out the conditions for switching to that approach early if the administrator request stalls, since it is work that would be kept either way.
  7. Flagged that the existing listing feature relies on a signed-in user for its security check, so opening it to the chat platform needs a deliberate replacement rather than a bypass.

1. Reviewed a proposal to run website page migrations through a chat assistant instead of purpose-built screens, and worked through where it was right and where it needed changing.
  2. Confirmed which version of the self-hosted chat platform is actually running on the company server, closing an open question about whether it supports the features the whole plan depends on.
  3. Argued against building a throwaway prototype that would have been deleted a stage later, and agreed to validate with permanent pieces instead.
  4. Agreed to keep file uploads out of chat for the first version, which removed two of the riskiest unknowns from the critical path.
  5. Raised a gap in the proposal — nothing prevented the assistant from accidentally starting the same expensive migration twice — and agreed on a fix.
  6. Settled that the chat assistant should read project repositories directly rather than routing through the existing migration service, which changed how per-project access is designed.
  7. Agreed to continue testing the current low-cost language model for tool use rather than switching to a more expensive one, since evaluating that model is the point of the exercise.

name: Reviewing the Chat Platform Migration Proposal

notes:
1. Investigated the existing automated page-migration system end to end — how a migration is triggered from the app, how the automated pipeline builds and verifies the page, and how results, costs, and publish steps flow back.
  2. Researched the newly deployed Open WebUI platform against its official documentation, verifying current capabilities: request flow, tools, knowledge, prompts, skills, external integrations, webhooks, and patterns for long-running jobs.
  3. Confirmed several up-to-date platform facts that changed the design: the older plugin server is now considered legacy, reusable skills are now a built-in feature, and native tool calling is the new default.
  4. Compared the current GitHub-Actions-based workflow with Open WebUI's capabilities to identify similarities, gaps, advantages, and simplification opportunities.
  5. Recommended an architecture where Open WebUI becomes the chat-based control layer while the existing automated pipeline remains the execution engine, keeping the current app as the system of record and staying model-agnostic so providers can be swapped later.
  6. Wrote a three-phase implementation plan with risks, unknowns to validate, and open questions, and saved the full proposal as a self-contained document in the project for continuing the work on another computer.
  7. Recorded the product decisions into the document: hosting on Coolify, a chat-first direction for business developers, internal operators only for now, publish-from-chat gated behind a two-step confirmation, one shared instance during testing, and DeepSeek as the initial model.
  8. Clarified that the deployed Open WebUI instance almost certainly runs from the official prebuilt image with no forked source repository, and advised versioning its configuration as exported artifacts rather than maintaining a fork.

notes:
1. Investigated why every recent production deploy of the page builder app was failing — builds compiled fine, but the hosting platform refused to create the serverless functions because the combined size of the environment settings exceeded the cloud provider's hard 4KB limit.
  2. Identified the exact production site affected by matching the team's hosted sites against the code repository and the branch being deployed.
  3. Audited all 52 environment settings on the site, measuring each one's size and where it gets used, and found nearly all of them were being packed into every serverless function — leaving no room for the values the platform adds on its own.
  4. Cross-checked every setting against the codebase and confirmed most are genuinely required while the app runs, so they could not be removed.
  5. Found two settings that are not used anywhere in the code and one that only matters during builds, and excluded just those three from the function runtime — keeping their values intact and saving a rollback record so the change can be undone instantly.
  6. Confirmed the recently added AI service key was only the tipping point — the budget was already nearly full before it was added.
  7. Triggered a fresh deploy after the cleanup and verified it succeeded: all nine background functions were created and the live site and its sign-in service respond normally.
  8. Walked through where to validate the fix in the hosting dashboard — deploy logs, the functions log viewer, and the environment settings screen.
  9. Recorded project guidance so future environment settings are only exposed to functions when actually needed, preventing a repeat of the failure.

notes:
1. Investigated a report that newly created enterprise sites only allowed domain settings on one hosting provider, and confirmed the domain controls for the second provider were always disabled even though enterprise sites are deployed to both.
  2. Found the root cause: the check that decides which provider's domain settings are editable was hardcoded by plan type and completely ignored the primary-provider flag saved when the site is created.
  3. Enabled domain editing and the go-live action for both hosting providers on enterprise sites, while keeping business sites limited to their single deployed provider.
  4. Changed how the active provider is determined so the saved primary flag now takes priority, with the plan type kept as a fallback for older records that never had the flag set.
  5. Updated the go-live process so promoting a domain on one provider removes the primary mark from the other, guaranteeing only one provider is ever treated as primary.
  6. Fixed a hidden bug where reverting a domain that was never live could wrongly erase the site's live domain and reset the studio address.
  7. Updated the status badges so the "Primary" label follows the provider actually serving the live domain instead of being fixed by plan type.
  8. Verified the changed files compile cleanly, and documented false alarms from a misconfigured automated code checker so future work isn't misled by them.

notes:
1. Investigated why the automated page-migration pipeline failed to open pull requests and found that GitHub blocks its built-in automation identity from creating pull requests unless a specific organization setting is switched on.
  2. Clarified how a shared personal access token created under one organization could also serve the other organization, including which token types can and cannot cross organization boundaries.
  3. Established that newly created site repositories arrive with the pull-request permission setting off by default, and laid out the options for handling that across auto-provisioned projects.
  4. Decided to replace personal access tokens with a single GitHub App installed on both organizations, which avoids the permission restriction entirely and is not tied to any individual's account.
  5. Explained how one app with a single key serves both organizations — each organization gets its own installation, and the access minted at runtime is automatically confined to the organization where the pipeline runs.
  6. Updated the migration pipeline so it authenticates with the GitHub App, minting its short-lived access late in the run because the pipeline can outlast the access lifetime, with graceful fallback to the older methods if the app is not configured.
  7. Fixed a hidden pitfall where credentials saved at the start of the run would silently override the new access during the final publish step.
  8. Verified the newly created app is publicly installable, and spotted that it is owned by a personal account rather than the organization — recommended transferring ownership for continuity.
  9. Walked through the remaining setup outside the code: installing the app on both organizations and storing the app credentials once per organization so every site inherits them.
  10. Simplified the credential setup by storing both app values as secrets in one place, updating the pipeline to match.
  11. Clarified that the old personal access token is now only a backup that no longer needs to be created or maintained.

notes:
1. Reworked the section-building skill so it can run reliably start-to-finish on its own in automated pipelines, where there is no chance to correct course mid-run.
  2. Added a clear set of completion rules that define exactly what "done" means and require a final report before the run can end, so unattended runs can't stop halfway and claim success.
  3. Added a strict safety rule that changes must be left uncommitted for the developer to review first, so nothing is ever committed or pushed automatically no matter how the run was started.
  4. Clarified that the section-building procedure must be followed in full no matter which entry point kicks it off, so a wrapping shortcut can't quietly skip the required steps and checks.
  5. Added guidance for handling mockups that are saved as packaged snapshots, explaining how to pull out the real design and images instead of mistakenly reading the loading-screen styling and producing garbage.
  6. Built in a requirement to run mechanical verification scripts whose pass/fail verdicts override the agent's own self-assessment, so a real failure can never be reported as a pass.
  7. Cleaned up and reformatted the reference documentation tables and formatting for consistency and readability.

notes:
1. Added an automatic setup step during new site creation that provisions the secret keys the Claude implementation workflow needs — the AI service key, the dataset name, and the read and write access tokens — directly onto the new site's code repository.
  2. Built a new server endpoint that returns the list of projects a given email address owns or belongs to, so the scraper app can determine which projects a signed-in user is allowed to connect.
  3. Made project membership lookups include pending invitations, so a project becomes connectable as soon as an invite is sent rather than only after it is accepted.
  4. Gave backend administrators the ability to see and resolve all projects by email, regardless of ownership or membership.
  5. Tightened security on the studio lookup endpoint by making its internal access key mandatory — the endpoint now refuses every request when the key is not configured, instead of running unprotected.
  6. Added email normalization so project lookups match reliably regardless of how the address is typed in.

notes:
1. Reviewed all the changes on the page-migration branch against the project's existing security audit to check whether anything new introduced a risk.
  2. Ran a full security review of the branch and confirmed a real cross-account vulnerability in the new migration feature.
  3. Found that the migration actions trusted the target code repository sent by the browser instead of confirming it belonged to the user's own project — meaning a logged-in user could read from, upload files to, or trigger automated work on another customer's repository.
  4. Fixed the vulnerability by making the server decide the allowed repository from the user's own project, so a mismatched repository can no longer be supplied from the request.
  5. Added a safety check that rejects any repository name containing unusual path characters, as an extra layer of protection.
  6. Confirmed the fix did not break the other migration screens and that the changed files were free of errors.

  3. Found that the migration actions trusted the target code repository sent by the browser instead of confirming it belonged to the user's own project — meaning a logged-in user could read from, upload files to, or trigger automated work on another customer's repository.
  4. Fixed the vulnerability by making the server decide the allowed repository from the user's own project, so a mismatched repository can no longer be supplied from the request.
  5. Added a safety check that rejects any repository name containing unusual path characters, as an extra layer of protection.
  6. Confirmed the fix did not break the other migration screens and that the changed files were free of errors.
name: Migration Repository Access Vulnerability Fix

notes:
1. Traced the entire site-creation process to pinpoint exactly where a new site's code repository is set up and where its secure credentials are added.
  2. Confirmed that the platform already adds encrypted credentials to each new site's repository during creation, while other configuration is sent to the hosting providers rather than stored on the repository itself.
  3. Identified that the platform had no way to add plain, non-secret repository settings — only encrypted credentials — and noted this for a variable that is not actually sensitive.
  4. Discovered that some of the requested credentials were not yet present in the application's own settings, and flagged this so the values would not be added empty.
  5. Extended site creation so every newly created site automatically receives the credentials its automated assistant workflow needs, reusing the existing secure credential process instead of building a separate one.
  6. Named the new setup step to match the naming style already used for similar setup steps, so it reads clearly alongside them.
  7. Verified that site-specific read and write access tokens are already generated earlier in the creation process, and switched the two access credentials to use those site-scoped tokens instead of shared application-wide ones.
  8. Confirmed the change keeps existing sites and workflows working unchanged, since it only adds a new step that runs for newly created sites.

notes:
1. Investigated why a signed-in user in the scraper app was seeing a full list of customer projects that did not belong to them.
  2. Traced how the app decides which projects a user is allowed to see, following the path from the app's project list, through the membership check, to the main platform's lookup of projects by email.
  3. First suspected a recently added rule that lets platform administrators see every project, and confirmed with the user whether that was the intended behavior.
  4. Ruled out the administrator explanation after the user confirmed the signed-in email is not a registered user on the platform at all, which meant the server should have returned no projects.
  5. Re-examined the app and found that the project list is stored in the browser's local cache under a single shared name, with no separation between different user accounts.
  6. Confirmed the cached list is kept for one hour and is shown immediately without asking the server, and that it is never cleared when a user signs out or switches accounts.
  7. Concluded the real cause: a stale, shared browser cache from an earlier session was displaying another account's project list, even though the server was correctly returning nothing for the current user.
  8. Gave the user a quick way to confirm the finding in the browser and recommended a two-part fix — separating the cache per user account and clearing it on sign-out — since this is a genuine cross-account data exposure.

notes:
1. Planned and documented a project to unify the two website-migration workflows — importing from a live website URL and uploading exported HTML files — into one cohesive product experience, including a full written task plan with requirements, acceptance criteria, and rollback notes.
  2. Walked both user journeys end to end and redesigned the experience around them: the dashboard becomes the home surface, users pick their migration source when creating a project, and the app routes them to the right workflow automatically.
  3. Found and fixed the core navigation bug on this branch where clicking any project always opened the HTML-migration screen, which had broken the original URL-based workflow for existing projects.
  4. Added a database field that records each project's migration type, with all existing projects safely defaulting to the legacy type so nothing changes for them.
  5. Built a project-creation source picker with two selectable cards — "Website URL" and "HTML files" — each with a short description, and form copy that updates with the selection so users always know what happens next.
  6. Made the dashboard project cards real links with type badges and a next-step hint, so keyboard navigation, opening in a new tab, and at-a-glance orientation all work.
  7. Built a shared progress strip shown on both workflow pages that displays the journey steps (done, current, upcoming) with counts and one contextual action button, so users always know where they are and what to do next.
  8. Consolidated the duplicated project header into a single shared component used by both workflow pages, and added a "Migrate pages" button so URL projects can also reach the HTML workflow easily.
  9. Put the HTML-migration page behind sign-in — it was previously reachable without logging in.
  10. Improved feedback and wording throughout: an honest "Scanning…" message during slow site scans, a friendlier empty state that points users back to their dashboard, clearer browser-tab title, and back links that say where they lead.
  11. Ran a quality review pass over everything built: merged duplicated data-fetching logic into one shared helper, removed an unused import and leftover debug logging, and confirmed the production build passes.
  12. Fixed a bug found during testing where HTML project names containing spaces were saved in a scrambled, percent-encoded form (for example "WebriQ Demo 2026" displayed as an encoded string); names are now stored exactly as typed, and a one-line database fix was provided for the record created before the fix.

notes:
1. Completed the failure analysis that was paused yesterday for the automated PipelineForge page migration — the run that ended with a failing verdict, no pull request, and no completion report.
  2. Retrieved the failed run's full transcript and diagnostic archives directly from the build service and traced the run event by event to pinpoint where it stopped.
  3. Found the true cause: the AI split the page into eleven section-building helpers running in the background at once and then sat idle waiting; two helpers' completion signals were never delivered, so the process decided nothing was left to do and shut down cleanly mid-migration — before integration, the quality checks, and the completion report.
  4. Confirmed the build work itself had actually finished — all eleven sections were built and preserved on the work-in-progress branch, and the page content was saved to the content database — so the next attempt can reuse it instead of starting over.
  5. Verified the previous attempt earlier that afternoon died the same way, quitting immediately after starting its helpers, which proved this is a repeatable flaw in how the run waits on helpers rather than a random glitch.
  6. Ruled out the suspected culprits: yesterday's new prompt safeguards and the change to commit attribution played no role, and memory, disk space, timeouts, and provider errors were all cleared as well.
  7. Identified a contributing gap: the pipeline never gave the AI any way to check on background helpers, leaving idle waiting — the exact move that kills the run — as its only option.
  8. Strengthened the instructions given to the automated pipeline: helpers must now run in the foreground and the AI may never end its turn while a helper is still working.
  9. Updated the pipeline configuration to grant the AI the tools needed to check on background helpers, as a backstop in case one runs in the background anyway.
  10. Verified both fixes pass their validation checks and left them uncommitted for review, noting the instruction fix takes effect once the app is deployed and the configuration fix once it reaches the main branch.
  11. Flagged that the operational guide's embedded copy of the migration instructions has fallen out of date and offered to bring it in sync.

notes:
1. Investigated whether the sequential migration option could be removed in favor of always running pages in parallel, now that the client repo automatically merges overlapping additions to the shared task tracker file.
  2. Found the removal would not be safe: GitHub ignores that auto-merge setting when merging pull requests through its own service, which is exactly how the app's "Ship it" step merges — so conflicts would still block shipping.
  3. Confirmed the task tracker is not the only shared file — each migrated page also adds entries to shared component and schema registries in the client site, which would still conflict during parallel runs.
  4. Noted a third reason to keep sequential mode: parallel runs cannot see each other's work, so two runs can accidentally build the same section twice.
  5. Recommended keeping both the auto-merge setting and the sequential option, and outlined what would need to change before parallel-only migration becomes safe.
  6. Replaced the "Migrate sequentially" checkbox with a confirmation popup — clicking the migrate button with two or more pages selected now asks whether to run them one at a time (recommended) or all at once, with a plain description of each option's trade-off.
  7. Made single-page migrations skip the popup and start immediately, since the choice makes no difference for one page.
  8. Added a hint under the selection controls letting users know the mode choice comes next, and made canceling the popup keep the page selection intact.
  9. Updated the on-page help text plus the workflow and task documents to describe the new choice, including refreshed acceptance criteria and a testing checklist.
  10. Verified the app compiles cleanly with the change; the only build failure is a known local setup issue unrelated to this work.

notes:
1. Investigated why the automated PipelineForge page migration failed in the build pipeline — found the AI run produced no output at all and quit after about ninety seconds, rather than failing any of the quality checks.
  2. Retrieved and analyzed the failed run's logs and archives, ruling out memory, disk-space, and timeout causes; confirmed the AI provider returned an empty answer, a known intermittent glitch with the outside model being used.
  3. Discovered that an earlier successful migration of the same page had been rejected and closed just minutes before the failed re-run, and that partial leftover content from that earlier attempt is still sitting in the content database; flagged the leftovers so the next attempt reuses them instead of creating duplicates.
  4. Recommended simply re-running the migration since the failure was a random model glitch rather than a setup problem.
  5. Added live progress logging to the migration pipeline so every action the AI takes appears in the build log while the run is happening, instead of the log staying silent until the very end.
  6. Built and tested a formatter that turns the AI's machine-readable event stream into short, readable progress lines, verifying it against both sample data and a live test run.
  7. Added clear failure explanations to the pipeline: what the exit code means, an explicit warning when the AI returns an empty answer, and the completion report shown directly on the run's summary page so failures no longer require downloading archives to diagnose.
  8. Added diagnostics to the relay that sits between the pipeline and the AI provider so it now records whether each response contained usable content — making the empty-answer failure instantly visible in the future.
  9. Caught that the new log formatter had been left out of the changes pushed to the repository, which caused the next pipeline run to fall back to unreadable raw logs, and explained why it needs to be included.
  10. Began investigating a second failed migration run that behaved differently — it worked for about twenty-five minutes but never produced its completion report; the analysis was paused midway at the user's request.

notes:
1. Investigated a client page created by the automated migration pipeline that appeared to be missing sections and data; confirmed the generated code and content were actually complete by running the project's automated design-comparison checks, which all passed.
  2. Found the real cause of the missing content: the preview website was reading from a different content database than the one the pipeline wrote to, so it displayed a stale, abandoned migration attempt from two weeks earlier.

notes:
1. Investigated why the project connection dialog reported no project found for a project the user owns — traced it to an earlier security fix that limited the dropdown to already-connected projects, which made first-time connections impossible.
  2. Built a search fallback that let users find unconnected projects by typing part of the name, with limits in place so the full client project list could not be exposed.
  3. Added an admin allowlist giving operator accounts the full project list; removed it after review because managing access through environment settings was judged unsustainable.
  4. Replaced it with membership-based visibility: the app now shows a project when the signed-in user's email is a member of it on the content platform, so inviting someone is all that is needed to grant access.
  5. Confirmed the membership approach against live production data covering roughly 550 projects and 700 memberships before writing the code.
  6. Simplified the implementation by consolidating duplicated server logic into one shared module and removing unnecessary complexity from the search interface.
  7. Removed the search fallback at the user's request so project visibility is now purely invite-driven, fully restoring the original security protections.
  8. Diagnosed why a revoked project still appeared after logging out — the browser keeps a cached copy of the project list for an hour and logout does not clear it — and explained how to clear it.
  9. Discovered that member invitations sent from the StackShift app do not carry over to the content platform, which was why the user's earlier invites never took effect.
  10. Sent a proper invitation directly through the content platform on the user's behalf and verified the accepted membership registered with administrator access.
  11. Wrote the required task documentation and updated the project tracker to reflect the work.

notes: The day's migration work focused on making the links shown for finished page migrations trustworthy and useful. The preview address problem was solved at the root: instead of guessing a web address that often didn't exist, the app now asks the hosting platform directly for the real deployment address, stores it, self-heals older broken records on refresh, and deep-links straight to the migrated page. Building on that, the branch name shown on each finished migration became a working link as well — after discovering that pull request addresses aren't recorded until a migration ships, the label was pointed at the branch's own page on the code hosting site, which works immediately for past and unshipped migrations without any server changes. Each finished migration now offers two distinct, reliable links: one to the code branch and one to the live preview. Documentation, configuration notes, and verification checks accompanied the changes.

notes: The day was spent diagnosing and repairing the automated page-migration pipeline after a run failed without producing a review branch or pull request despite doing real work. The root cause was that the AI model's hidden reasoning made the automation print an empty final answer, so the success check misread a completed run as a failure — and a previously built fix turned out to have been accidentally wiped from the project before it was ever used. The validated fix was recovered from earlier session records, wired into the pipeline with safety checks, and the pipeline was changed to always preserve a failed run's work on a clearly marked review branch so website content can no longer be stranded without its matching code. The repairs were verified end to end through configuration checks, simulated success and failure scenarios, a live model test, and repeated back-and-forth testing between the app's interface and the automation run data. Leftover orphaned content from the two failed runs was inventoried and flagged for manual cleanup, documentation was updated to match the new behavior, and all changes were left uncommitted for review.

notes: The day centered on making the automated page-migration pipeline trustworthy and its results visible. A falsely failed homepage migration was traced to the build machine running out of memory at the finish line, and later diagnostics uncovered two more silent killers — a disk that filled to zero and an AI model whose entire answer arrived as hidden reasoning text — each of which was fixed or given a working countermeasure, including a locally proven relay that strips the hidden content so the DeepSeek model can be used. The pipeline itself was hardened with durable completion reports, freed disk space, health monitoring, a rule that a run with no pull request now shows as failed, and a two-stage smoke test that can be triggered from the web app to pinpoint which layer is broken. On the product side, migration pages gained persistent custom web-address names with a confirmation step, and mockup uploads now require confirmation with clear duplicate-replacement warnings instead of silently overwriting existing files. An audit of the PipelineForge page found all built sections present in code but never pushed live, along with a missing section, broken navigation pieces, and uneditable text that still need follow-up.

notes:
1. Added stage-by-stage progress notifications to the automated page-migration pipeline so the requesting app can show a live progress view: branch created, AI run started and finished, completion report checked, changes published, pull request opened, and final completion.
  2. Built a small shared notification helper that formats each progress message safely, so specially crafted text from outside cannot break the message structure, and verified it produces valid messages using a test stand-in for the network call.
  3. Captured the new pull request's web address during the run and included it in the progress and completion notifications so the app can link straight to the human review page.
  4. Clarified that the preview site deployment starts automatically when the branch is published, and made the completion notification carry enough detail for the app to locate that deployment.
  5. Investigated a pipeline failure where the AI step was terminated from the outside partway through, which silently skipped every remaining step including the result check and failure notification.
  6. Added a time limit around the AI run itself so a stuck or overlong run now ends cleanly and the pipeline still reports a result instead of being killed by the outer job limit.
  7. Made the result-checking step run even when earlier steps are killed, so a verdict, a saved log, and a failure notification always reach the app no matter how the run dies.
  8. Narrowed the failure cause using the timing: the run died after roughly eleven minutes while healthy runs take one to two hours, pointing to an early kill — most likely memory exhaustion on the hosted machine or the AI terminating its own processes — rather than a timeout.
  9. Added self-diagnosis to the pipeline: the AI run's output now streams live into the job log, memory usage is sampled every half minute, and system kernel messages are captured at the end, all saved alongside the run's log files for post-mortem review.

notes:
1. Diagnosed why the automated page-migration pipeline failed at its very first step: it required a repository access token that was never configured, so it received an empty value and stopped immediately.
  2. Fixed the failure by letting the pipeline fall back to GitHub's built-in access token whenever the personal access token secret is missing, so runs no longer break on that setup gap.
  3. Granted the pipeline the specific write permissions the built-in token needs to publish the preview branch and open the pull request at the end of a run.
  4. Cleared the Node 20 deprecation warning by upgrading the pipeline's building-block steps to versions that run on the newer Node 24 runtime, while keeping the application's own Node version unchanged per project standards.
  5. Verified the updated pipeline configuration file is still valid and well-formed.
  6. Documented a trade-off of the fallback: pull requests opened with the built-in token do not trigger the automated browser test suite, and recommended configuring the personal access token to restore that behavior.

notes:
1. Added a manual run option to the automated page-migration pipeline so it can be tested directly from the GitHub website, without needing the requesting application to exist yet.
  2. Unified how the pipeline reads its parameters so manually entered values and app-sent values flow through one shared path, which also closed the last places where externally supplied text was inserted unsafely into scripts.
  3. Confirmed the pipeline will appear in the GitHub Actions list as soon as it reaches the main branch, and clarified it will show no runs and no manual-run button until triggered — which motivated adding the manual run option.
  4. Documented the minimal permissions for the pipeline's access token: repository content and pull-request access only, scoped to this single repository, with everything else denied.
  5. Identified that leaving workflow-editing permission off the token doubles as a safety guarantee — an automated run can never modify the pipeline itself.
  6. Reworked the pipeline to reuse an already-configured repository secret for the content platform's project ID instead of requiring a duplicate under a new name, reducing setup work.
  7. Renamed the read and write credential secrets to drop the public-facing prefix, keeping credential names visually distinct from non-sensitive settings, and documented the final list of five secrets to configure.

notes:
1. Investigated a live migration run whose progress display was stuck on "processing" — pulled the failed cloud run's step-by-step results and full logs directly from the automation service to find out what happened.
  2. Found the build machine was shut down by the platform about eighteen minutes into the AI build step, almost certainly from memory exhaustion — the same failure mode identified the previous session.
  3. Confirmed the failed run had launched from an older version of the automation that predated the memory protections, and that the current published version already includes all the hardening — so the next run is already covered.
  4. Pinpointed why the display stayed stuck: when the machine died, the steps that report failure back to the app were skipped entirely, so the app never heard the run had ended.
  5. Unstuck the display by manually sending the failure notification the dead run never sent, and confirmed the app accepted it and marked the run as failed.
  6. Identified a remaining weakness: even the hardened automation cannot report failure if its machine is killed outright, and laid out two possible fixes for the user to choose from.
  7. Implemented the chosen fix — failure reporting now runs as its own separate follow-up step on a fresh machine, so the app gets notified no matter how badly the main run died, including a previously uncovered case where the build succeeded but publishing the results failed.
  8. Validated the updated automation configuration and left the change ready for review and publishing, and explained the purpose of the safety time limit on the new follow-up step.

notes:
1. Clarified that the callback address browser error was expected behavior — the endpoint only accepts machine-to-machine posts, and reaching it at all proved the deployment was healthy.
  2. Discovered the hosting platform's deployment protection was silently blocking the automation's status callbacks, by probing the preview deployment the same way the automation would call it.
  3. Wired up the protection bypass: the user created a bypass secret, the dispatch flow now attaches it to every callback address, and a live probe confirmed callbacks get through the protection wall.
  4. Fixed a bug where a trailing slash in the configured site address produced a malformed callback address that the automation's status reports would silently bounce off.
  5. Investigated two failed automation runs by pulling their full logs, and found the root cause: the cloud build machine itself was shut down mid-run — most likely from memory exhaustion — rather than any script or model error.
  6. Added a memory cap to the automation so runaway memory now crashes cleanly and reports failure, instead of taking down the whole machine and leaving the app with no status update.
  7. Diagnosed why the progress display stayed stuck on the first step during a live run: the improved automation with progress reporting was never published, and that run's callback address pointed at the local machine, which the cloud cannot reach.
  8. Audited the hosting platform's environment settings and confirmed every key the preview deployment needs is in place, and that the newest build includes all the recent fixes.
  9. Interpreted the hosting platform's traffic logs for the user, showing they only contained the UI's own polling — consistent with the finding that no callback had ever successfully arrived.
  10. Built live stage tracking end to end: the database now stores which pipeline stage a run is in, the callback records stage progress with safeguards against out-of-order updates, and the UI checks off each of the seven steps in real time — with failures now pointing at the stage that actually broke.
  11. Agreed on the launch checklist for the next test: apply the database change first, then publish the app and automation updates, then trigger a migration from the preview site.

  3. Fixed a reversed recipient check in the escalation email service that could validate against the wrong mailbox.
  4. Debugged why no email arrived when a visitor asked to talk to a representative: the request and the visitor's email address arrive in separate chat messages, and the request was being forgotten in between.
  5. Built a fix that remembers a pending hand-off request and sends the team notification as soon as the visitor shares their email in a later message; failed sends are kept so a later message retries them.

  8. Added clear log messages showing whether an escalation email was sent, failed, or stored as pending, so future email issues are visible instead of silent.

  2. Investigated errors on the PipelineForge page in the content editor where the new sections were flagged as invalid, and confirmed the page content and local setup were actually correct.
  3. Identified the cause of those errors: the live editor was running an older build that did not yet include the new section definitions, because the recent work had not been committed or deployed.
  4. Verified all PipelineForge content in the CMS matched the expected section names, ruling out any data problem on that page.
  5. Diagnosed a separate error on the bookstore page where every section was stored with a generic reference label instead of its proper section name, which made the sections uneditable.
  6. Repaired the bookstore page by correcting all seven section entries directly in the CMS and confirmed the fix took effect.
  7. Traced the bad bookstore data to a source outside this project — none of the project's own migration scripts produced it.
  8. Found that four bookstore sections have no definitions in the project at all, and flagged that they must either be built properly or removed before that page is fully usable.
  9. Added a safeguard rule to the implementation workflow so future content writes are checked for the wrong-reference mistake before a task can be marked done.
  10. Closed a blind spot in the section-building checklist: its verification step could not detect this kind of broken data because it checked the wrong level; the check now catches it.
  11. Corrected a credential naming mismatch in the workflow docs that had caused an authentication failure during the repair.
  12. Clarified the new safeguard so it only applies to content-related tasks, keeping the implementation workflow safe and general-purpose for all other kinds of work.
name: Editor Error Diagnosis, Data Repair, and Safeguards

notes:
1. Verified the freshly regenerated plan for the new landing page and confirmed it passed review with zero hand edits — all fourteen page sections were correctly mapped, reuse decisions were justified with confidence scores, and content-only sections correctly carried no build documents of their own.
  2. Confirmed the plan's decision to reuse the site's existing brand blue instead of adding new colors was correct, by checking how previously shipped pages handled the same accent color.
  3. Closed a workflow gap where tracker entries for content-only sections could send an automated build session into a dead end with nothing to do, by clarifying that those entries are completed by the final integration step.
  4. Audited the first build of the announcement bar section and found it used raw page markup instead of the shared component library; traced the cause to the build copying an older shipped section as its example, and updated the standard to state that legacy code never overrides the rules.
  5. Discovered the project's code-style checker is broken in both of its invocation forms, meaning the component-usage rule could never be enforced automatically; made the working text-search check the official gate and corrected the guidance documents.
  6. Audited the rebuilt announcement bar and confirmed the code itself now fully meets the standard — proper shared components, correct colors, and exact content from the design file.
  7. Found the rebuild had also connected shared site files and run a content migration ahead of schedule, both reserved for the final integration step; reverted the shared-file changes and removed a stray content record and script it had created in the content database.
  8. Resolved a contradiction between two workflow rules — one demanding every build wire itself immediately, the other reserving wiring for the integration step — by adding a clear scope rule for which applies when.
  9. Added a rule that a task document's own status line must stay in sync with the project tracker, after the user noticed documents still marked as planned after work had started.
  10. Explained how content-migration scripts work in this workflow — they are run by the build agent during the integration step and verified with a read-back check, not automated by the project itself.
  11. Fully reset the tracker, task documents, and generated files back to the planned state so implementation can restart cleanly under the corrected rules.
  12. Produced the planning and implementation stages end to end through the company's coding tool to verify the reworked workflow in practice — generating the page plan and running the first section builds so every result could be audited against the standard and fed back into the workflow rules.

notes:
1. Investigated why an automated implementation task for a new landing page appeared stuck at the step that creates page content, and determined the work was actually running in a separate client project rather than the current one.
  2. Checked the live client content database and confirmed none of the expected page content had been created, proving the content-creation step never actually completed rather than just failing to update its progress checklist.
  3. Diagnosed an "unauthorized" error during content creation as the script not sending a valid access token, rather than a permissions problem, since reading data worked while writing failed.
  4. Verified the available access token was fully authorized to write to the client database by running a safe test that was immediately reversed, ruling out the credential as the cause.
  5. Explained how to correctly re-run the content-creation step, including making sure the access token is actually loaded when the script runs and approving the command if the other coding tool was waiting on it.
  6. Reviewed a generated page section and found it was hand-building raw web page elements instead of using the shared component library, and flagged that it also relied on many one-off styling values.
  7. Determined the root cause was that the "always use the shared components" rule existed only as written guidance with no automated check, so it was quietly ignored under a large set of instructions.
  8. Added an automated code rule and updated the section-building guide so using raw web page elements now fails an automated check instead of only being discouraged in writing.
  9. Applied these changes directly to the client project, adding the enforcement rule and updating the guide's build and verification steps.
  10. Discovered and fixed a pre-existing problem where the project's code-checking tool was completely non-functional due to a version mismatch, restoring the ability to check code quality at all.
  11. Fixed a small pre-existing error in a configuration file that had made it invalid.
  12. Confirmed the new rule correctly flags the problem section and measured the cleanup needed, finding a large amount of pre-existing content across the project that does not yet follow the standard.

notes:
1. Analyzed the scraper platform's full variant workflow — how it analyzes page sections, decides whether an existing design can be reused, generates new component code, and commits everything — to document its rules and safety checks.
  2. Rewrote the client site's section-building guide so pages built manually or by other coding tools produce the same commit structure and code quality as the automated scraper pipeline.
  3. Converted the pipeline's automatic error-repair steps into a mandatory pre-commit audit checklist in the guide, so weaker AI models catch the same mistakes the pipeline fixes automatically.
  4. Added previously missing wiring steps to the guide: registering new variants in the studio's variant picker, a crash guard for the studio's preview, and saving a preview image for every new variant so future builds can recognize and reuse existing designs.
  5. Documented the decision rules and confidence thresholds for when to reuse an existing design versus building a new variant, matching the automated pipeline's standards.
  6. Confirmed both build paths draw on the same installed component library, and added an explicit step to read reference code from the installed packages before writing any new component.
  7. Walked through the end-to-end workflow for converting HTML mockups into live pages, clarifying that pages appear in the studio as content records created through the platform's API rather than as files in the repository.
  8. Verified file-by-file that the guide's editing instructions match what the automated pipeline commits, confirming an existing custom section already follows the expected shape.
  9. Set up project permissions in the client repository so implementation runs proceed without asking for approval on every edit and command, while keeping publishing steps under manual review; recommended matching auto-approve settings for the other coding tool.
  10. Discovered the implementation stage never actually required reading the section-building guide; fixed this by adding a mandatory reading step and creating a missing entry-point document so every coding tool reliably loads the guide first.
  11. Reviewed the new PipelineForge page plan against the guide and the pipeline, flagging missing checklist items, misnumbered verification gates, and a structural difference in how the two flows categorize sections that could cause duplicate designs later.

notes:
1. Investigated how the "Active Sessions" figure on the conversations analytics dashboard is calculated and traced it from the database through to the number shown on the card.
  2. Found and fixed a caching bug that made Active Sessions — along with several other analytics figures — show zero whenever cached results were used, because the cache was reading a stale, mismatched set of saved fields.
  3. Identified that "Active Sessions" was actually counting any conversation where the visitor sent at least one message in the selected period, which did not match what the label implied.
  4. Redefined "Active Sessions" to mean sessions that are currently live — those with activity in the last 15 minutes — after confirming the intended meaning with the team.
  5. Made the live session count recalculate fresh on every request so it is never served from the hourly cache, since a cached "live now" number would be misleading.
  6. Updated the Active Sessions drill-down list and the card's description text so they match the new live definition.
  7. Added an automatic background refresh every 30 seconds so the live count decreases honestly as sessions age out, without needing to reload the page.
  8. Recommended a hybrid real-time approach — keeping expensive period totals cached while only the live count updates continuously — rather than recalculating everything in real time.
  9. Added handling so that a new message in an existing conversation updates the live count within a couple of seconds, while avoiding overcounting from rapid bursts of messages.
  10. Diagnosed why chatting in Test Chat did not move the analytics — test conversations are intentionally never saved to the database, so they cannot appear in analytics or trigger live updates.
  11. Confirmed the live-update system is correctly wired for real visitor conversations and provided ready-to-run database commands to simulate a live chat and verify the whole flow end to end.

  8. Verified the changes introduced no new errors by comparing against the project's pre-existing issues.
  9. Noted one deployment step for the team — applying the database change — and flagged a minor behavior change where the inline search panel now shows the typing text it previously omitted.

notes:
1. Researched and planned a new way for a separate trusted backend to request and receive a product information API key automatically, without anyone logging in through a browser.
  2. Decided that every key created this way should belong to a single locked-down service account rather than to individual people, which keeps access tightly controlled and limits damage if a key ever leaks.
  3. Chose to protect the new request endpoint with its own dedicated shared secret, kept completely separate from the normal user login keys.
  4. Worked through the security risks of the feature and decided on safeguards for each one, including limiting how often keys can be requested, keeping an audit record of every request, and allowing only approved network addresses to call it.
  5. Planned a smooth secret-rotation process so the shared secret can be replaced over time without any downtime or breaking the systems that rely on it.
  6. Agreed that newly created keys get the lowest sensible level of access by default and that the requester cannot ask for anything more powerful.
  7. Decided the plaintext key would be returned only once at creation and never stored or written into logs, so it cannot be recovered or exposed later.
  8. Wrote up the agreed design as reference documentation covering how a caller uses the new endpoint, the required configuration, and the secret-rotation steps, ahead of the actual build.
log_notes:
1. Researched and planned a new way for a separate trusted backend to request and receive a product information API key automatically, without anyone logging in through a browser.
  2. Decided that every key created this way should belong to a single locked-down service account rather than to individual people, which keeps access tightly controlled and limits damage if a key ever leaks.
  3. Chose to protect the new request endpoint with its own dedicated shared secret, kept completely separate from the normal user login keys.
  4. Worked through the security risks of the feature and decided on safeguards for each one, including limiting how often keys can be requested, keeping an audit record of every request, and allowing only approved network addresses to call it.
  5. Planned a smooth secret-rotation process so the shared secret can be replaced over time without any downtime or breaking the systems that rely on it.
  6. Agreed that newly created keys get the lowest sensible level of access by default and that the requester cannot ask for anything more powerful.
  7. Decided the plaintext key would be returned only once at creation and never stored or written into logs, so it cannot be recovered or exposed later.
  8. Wrote up the agreed design as reference documentation covering how a caller uses the new endpoint, the required configuration, and the secret-rotation steps, ahead of the actual build.
name: Service API Key Generation Planning

notes:
1. Explained how the tool's variant handling is split into two separate steps — the step that checks which variants are missing only analyzes a page and never changes a client site, while a distinct, separately triggered step is what actually generates and saves the new variants.
2. Clarified what happens when someone starts page creation — in the live environment one click runs the analysis, the variant check, and the variant saving together, whereas in the development environment those are separate buttons and the create action expects the analysis to have been done first.
3. Noted two important caveats: variant saving is skipped entirely for certain page types, and if variant saving fails the page is still created anyway rather than being blocked.
4. Wrote a planning document for a new fix covering the rule for how locally built sections must be registered on a client site, including a clear explanation of why the wrong registration form crashes the site.
5. Confirmed the affected files do not live in this project but in the client site the tool publishes to, and decided the right place to fix it was the generator itself so the repair happens automatically on the next publish.
6. Implemented the fix so that whenever the generator updates a client site's list of registered sections, it now cleans up every locally built entry that uses the wrong form — not just the one being added — preventing a known crash from ever surfacing.
7. Made sure the cleanup only affects locally built sections and deliberately leaves entries that come from the shared component library untouched, since those legitimately require the form being removed.
8. Tested the cleanup against several cases, confirming it repairs broken entries, leaves correct ones alone, ignores shared-library entries, and makes no further changes when run a second time.
9. Reviewed the change against the project's coding standards and confirmed it passed the quality gate with no issues and no deviations from the plan.

notes:
1. Reviewed a written analysis of a build failure on the connected client site caused by recently committed custom variants, and confirmed the diagnosis of the two underlying problems was correct.
2. Investigated the in-house tool that automatically generates and commits custom variants to client sites, to find why it produced the broken code so it could be prevented at the source.
3. Discovered the true cause of the main build error: an automated cleanup step in the generator was wrongly deleting a needed import from generated files, which left the code referring to something that no longer existed and crashed the site build every time a navigation variant was added.
4. Confirmed the second reported problem — a mismatch in how section components were registered — had already been resolved by earlier fixes, so no further work was needed there.
5. Corrected the cleanup step so it now keeps the imports the generated code actually relies on while still removing genuinely unused or invalid ones, fixing the recurring build failure at its origin.
6. Added a final safety check that inspects every generated file just before it is committed, automatically restores a missing required import when it can, and raises a clear alert when it cannot — so a broken build can never silently reach a client site again.
7. Tested the new safety check against the real failure case plus several look-alike situations to confirm it repairs genuinely broken files and leaves correct files untouched.
8. Recorded the root cause and the fix as a durable note for future reference, linking it to a previously documented issue in the same generator.

notes:
1. Completed a full manual validation pass on the StackShift release, verifying the combined result of six merged pull requests before sign-off.
2. Verified the agent content layer and Sanity backfill — agent pages render correctly with their search-engine metadata, and the scripts that generate the crawler, robots, and sitemap files all run cleanly.
3. Verified the new product pages that pull live data from PublishForge — confirmed they render with images and content, fall back gracefully when the connection is unavailable, and that the page-refresh webhook correctly rejects requests with missing or wrong security tokens.
4. Verified the AI traffic tracking middleware, the highest-risk change — confirmed it stays completely inactive when tracking is turned off, sets and reuses the visitor session cookie correctly, skips static files and excluded pages, and properly classifies human visitors, AI crawlers, and AI referrals while stripping sensitive details out of tracked links.
5. Verified the newsletter relay to PublishForge behaves safely whether or not the connection is configured, never failing the user-facing form even when the downstream service is unavailable.
6. Verified the shared UI component library update and the removal of the legacy e-commerce templates — confirmed the site still builds, the studio loads without errors, and the styling is intact.
7. Ran the final cross-cutting checks for the release — full build and startup, a performance spot-check, linting, and the existing automated test suite.
8. Diagnosed a server error on the website's PublishForge proxy — traced it to a configuration value where the PublishForge web address had been mistakenly set to a secret key, so the outgoing request failed because the destination was no longer a valid web address.
9. Set up the publishforgedemo website repository to pull in the latest changes from the shared site template, and resolved the merge conflicts that came up so the demo site is back in sync with the template.

2. Confirmed that product-name questions and price-range questions both work, and that product images display correctly in the chat.
3. Found and fixed a bug where shoppers asking for "cabinet knobs" got no results because the word "cabinet" never appears in product names — the assistant now falls back to the main product type and returns matches. Applied the fix to both the public widget chat and the main internal chat.
4. Discovered that knowledge-base search was silently failing on every request and quietly falling back to a weaker keyword search because of a misconfigured database setting, and wrote a database fix to restore proper semantic search.
5. Fixed a recurring error where the assistant's query-analysis step crashed because its response was being cut off mid-sentence, by increasing the allowed response length so it completes.
6. Created and extended a sample conversation in the conversations page so the work could be reviewed visually.
7. Probed the assistant on product finishes, stock status, and variants, and found three gaps: it can't name finishes in the public chat because that detail isn't included, it reports unpriced items as costing "$0", and it cuts off long variant lists.
8. Confirmed the chat can technically show multiple product images but was only ever showing one, then updated the assistant's instructions so it now shows a separate image for each distinct product, and verified that multiple images render.
9. Reviewed whether an image carousel could be used and explained that none currently exists in a reusable form for chat, along with what building one would involve.
10. Traced which parts of the system power the public widget chat versus the main internal chat to confirm each fix lands on the correct path.

notes:
1. Diagnosed why product pages were returning a service-unavailable error during refresh, tracing it to a missing access token in the production environment rather than a code bug.
2. Confirmed the failure was happening at the security check before any data was loaded, which explained the very fast error responses across every product.
3. Explained why the admin screen was misleadingly reporting product refreshes as "succeeded" even though they were actually failing downstream.
4. Identified the true cause of the false success report — the public product page was quietly catching upstream errors and treating them as "page not found" instead of surfacing the failure.
5. Fixed the product page so that real upstream failures are passed through instead of swallowed, allowing the refresh system to correctly mark them as failed and retry them later.
6. Preserved the correct behavior for genuinely removed products so they still show a clean "not found" page without being counted as failures.
7. Noted an added benefit that the fix prevents live products from being temporarily hidden from search during a brief outage.

name: Product Page Revalidation Failure Fix

notes:
1. Investigated whether the scheduled catalog sync, indexing, and page-refresh cycle would automatically put recently-loaded product photos onto the live product pages, and confirmed it would not — product photos are deliberately left out of the internal change-detection signal, so a photo arriving later is invisible to the system and never triggers a page refresh on its own.
2. Explained how product-photo loading actually runs — confirmed it happens automatically as the final step of each catalog sync, on the server, in the background, continuing on its own up to a safe per-run limit with the remainder picked up by the next sync.
3. Clarified that re-running the "Apply & Refresh" action with unchanged display settings would also fail to push newly-loaded photos live, since nothing would detect the photo as a change, so there was no working path to get the photos onto the pages.
4. Built a fix in two coordinated parts so newly-loaded product photos now flow to the live pages: the photo-loading step now queues each affected product for re-indexing, and the indexing step now notices when a product's stored photo differs from its newly-loaded one and rebuilds and refreshes that product's page instead of skipping it.
5. Made the fix safe against wasted work — products whose page already shows the correct photo are simply skipped — and scoped the refresh to only the changed pages rather than the whole catalog.
6. Confirmed the changes passed type-checking, with only pre-existing unrelated issues and nothing new from this work.
7. Explained the server-side execution model in plain terms — the browser only kicks off the work and the rest runs on its own server-to-server, so photo loading finishes even if the browser is closed — while noting the "Apply & Refresh" sequence is browser-driven and would pause its next step if the browser is closed mid-run.
8. Wrote a one-time catch-up script as a safety net to queue any products whose photos were already loaded before this fix shipped, so their pages can be refreshed too.
9. Walked through exactly how the indexing step now decides to process a queued product rather than skip it — by comparing the product's stored photo against its current one — and clarified that the queueing and the comparison must both be in place for the photos to reach the live pages.
10. Flagged that the catch-up script and an unrelated work-log change were not part of the staged set.

notes:

7. Cleaned up the documentation across the main project so it consistently refers to the correct product page address, while deliberately leaving alone a planning-document filename and references to a now-removed publishing method, since changing those would have been wrong or broken links.
8. Identified which references must never be blindly renamed — a real file's name and a retired feature's folder path — and explained why, rather than doing a sweeping find-and-replace that would cause damage.
9. Flagged that the actual page-fixing changes belong to the website template project and need their own separate commit there.

notes:
1. Ran a quality-standards review of the automatic product-retirement feature and confirmed the code was clean, flagging only one minor, acceptable structuring choice.
2. Ran several rounds of independent automated code review on the feature; an early round found that the rule for hiding retired products was applied in most places but not every place that lists or counts them, and fixed each missed spot.
3. Found and fixed a class of bugs where — because retirement updates several records that aren't saved together as a single unit — a failure partway through could permanently leave a removed product's page hidden while it still answered in chat (or the reverse); reordered the updates so any interruption self-corrects on the next sync.
4. Caught and corrected a mistake from one of my own earlier fixes: I had reordered those updates the wrong way, which would have left a discontinued product's page live forever — corrected it and wrote down the underlying rule so it isn't repeated.
5. Found that even after the ordering fix a rare interruption could still leave a returned product's page stuck on "not found", and fixed the indexing step so it now detects and repairs that state automatically.
6. Decided not to run the usual on-screen browser testing because this feature is back-end data plumbing with almost nothing visible to a user, and explained that the right verification is code review plus targeted logic tests plus a hands-on run against real data — rather than producing a hollow passing screen test.
7. In a final clean review pass, caught a side effect of an earlier fix where leftover work items for already-removed products were being marked as failures instead of simply skipped — which both inflated the error count and could stall the indexing queue — and fixed it so those items are quietly cleared.
8. Wrote a developer reference document for the retirement feature capturing how it works and the safety rules that must not be changed.
9. Wrote a retrospective of the multiple review rounds and added the most reusable lessons to the project's shared learnings file.
10. Updated the project's main guidance file and the customer-facing setup guide to explain the new retirement behavior, and corrected an outdated note that wrongly claimed removed products are kept forever.
11. Marked the feature as documented but not yet verified, and recommended a final review pass plus logic tests before release rather than shipping on an unverified fix.

name: Product Retirement Review Rounds and Documentation

notes:
1. Explained that the product catalog's text is assembled by the app's own templates from real catalog data — not written by an AI — and that the only outside-AI involvement is turning that finished text into search data.
2. Confirmed that the product page content itself is built deterministically by code, with no AI writing or embellishing any of it.
3. Advised on whether to add AI-written product guidance, recommending the deterministic approach stay in place for public pages to avoid invented product claims and keep pages stable, with AI only considered later if product search matching proves weak.
4. Reviewed the code-review findings document and laid out clearly which items genuinely need to be addressed before release versus which are safe to defer.
5. Assessed the original product plan's unmet goals and concluded most were either intentional improvements, already handled, or an optional future enhancement — with the one real correctness gap already built.
6. Created a short plain-language document explaining why the richer AI-written guidance was deferred, intended for sharing with a senior.
7. Walked through what happens when a sync runs while some products are already gone from the supplier catalog, clarifying the two-pass safety delay before anything is retired.
8. Investigated whether a product returning to the catalog with no existing search entry gets re-added, and traced the exact paths that re-create it.
9. Identified a genuine corner case where a live product page could exist with no matching search entry — reachable only by manual data removal — that would otherwise never correct itself.
10. Implemented a fix so the sync now re-queues such products and the indexing step automatically re-inserts the missing search entry, while deliberately excluding empty placeholder products to avoid needless repeated work.
11. Verified the fix passed type-checking and code-style checks with no new issues.
12. Documented the new self-healing behavior in the project's planning notes, including its safeguards and small added cost.
13. Confirmed the end-to-end behavior with the team: removed products are retired and their pages return "not found", new products are queued on the next sync, and indexing and page-refresh re-add them — noting this is fully automatic only for scheduled syncs, while a manual sync still needs the indexing and refresh steps run.

name: Catalog Enrichment Review and Missing-Entry Self-Heal

notes:
1. Analyzed the two remaining gaps from the original product plan — richer AI-written buying guidance, and handling for products removed from the catalog — and recommended treating removal handling as a real correctness fix while keeping the richer guidance as an optional future enhancement.
2. Found that because the catalog sync already pulls the entire product list on every run, detecting removed products needs no new scheduled job and no extra calls to the supplier — it can be done as a simple comparison at the end of each full sync.
3. Wrote a detailed plan for automatically retiring products that disappear from the catalog, with safeguards so a single bad or partial sync can never wipe the whole catalog by mistake.
4. Built the automatic retirement feature: products missing across two consecutive full syncs are quietly hidden, their pages return "not found," and they stop appearing in chat answers — and products that reappear are automatically restored.
5. Explained how to remove or retire a product, clarifying that it is done in the source catalog rather than inside this app, and that simply marking a product inactive there does not currently hide its page.
6. Ran a quality review of the retirement feature and, during it, added protection so very large removal batches are processed safely without hitting database request-size limits or leaving products in a half-removed state.
7. Ran a thorough automated code review of the retirement feature using multiple independent reviewers, which surfaced nine confirmed issues.
8. Fixed the most serious finding — the development-only "test sync" button could have accidentally retired an entire catalog — by locking retirement to genuine full syncs only.
9. Fixed a case where a product coming back into stock could keep showing a "not found" page, by making sure restored products get their pages refreshed in the same run.
10. Fixed several supporting issues from the review — consistently excluding retired products everywhere they are listed or counted, preventing a rare case that could falsely retire live products, and consolidating duplicated logic into a shared, safer helper.
11. Wrote a separate, clearly-scoped plan capturing the richer AI-written product guidance as a future enhancement, keeping it distinct from the work already done.
12. Reorganized the planning documents so the removal feature and its review fixes are tracked as one unified task instead of two overlapping ones.

name: Discontinued Product Handling and Review Follow-Up

notes:
1. Walked through the product-pipeline code review findings and explained, in priority order, exactly what still needed fixing versus what was already handled.
2. Fixed a database-integrity bug where the safeguard that keeps one product record per item was only created during an upgrade path and never on a fresh install — moved it so it always runs, and added a one-time cleanup that removes leftover duplicate and orphaned product records before the safeguard is applied.
3. Hardened the product-catalog address safety checks against spoofing tricks that could trick the system into calling internal or cloud-metadata addresses (extra protection against a known class of server-side request attacks), and closed a couple of edge cases like disguised local addresses.
4. Added time limits to outbound product-catalog requests and to the analysis model call so a slow or hung external service can no longer stall a customer chat — it now falls back to existing knowledge instead.
5. Added proper input validation to the product-catalog admin save and sync endpoints so malformed requests are rejected cleanly.
6. Removed an unused, dead piece of widget code, corrected a misleading comment about how product attributes are matched, and made the public widget respect the on/off switch so a disabled catalog no longer triggers live product lookups.
7. Reconciled a large amount of documentation that pointed at database migration files that no longer exist after the team consolidated everything into a single migration — added a clear note explaining the consolidation and corrected each dangling reference.
8. Discovered that the earlier-flagged broken product-image rendering was already correctly fixed in the website template (the image host is allow-listed and the image component is set up properly), so confirmed it rather than duplicating the fix, and noted the deployed customer sites still need that template update rolled out.
9. Updated the code review findings document so every item reflects its current status — what is fixed, what is already done elsewhere, what is intentionally deferred, and what remains a cross-repository or product decision.
